name: Swiss / International Style
one_line: Fixed baseline grid; hierarchy by weight/size/position, never color.
palette_hint: true black + paper white + ONE saturated accent (often red H25-35); tint neutrals ≤C0.01

type.notes: one family carries all sizes; weights (regular/bold) do the hierarchy work; flush-left ragged-right; no italics for emphasis; tabular figures for any numerals.

grammar: Fixed baseline grid applies to every element including images — image crops snap to grid lines, never floating off-grid.
Hierarchy is expressed primarily through type weight, size, and position — color is not used to indicate importance.
Body copy is flush-left, ragged-right; full justification is never used.
Column widths are asymmetric but derived mathematically from the grid module, never eyeballed.
Typically one saturated accent color anchors the system; everything else is true black, true white, or a near-neutral tint.
first_viewport: A fixed 8-column grid fills the viewport edge-to-edge; a thin horizontal rule sits at one-third height carrying the wordmark flush-left and a single red rule-bounded link flush-right, with body copy beginning immediately below in a 6-column measure.

motion.moment: Grid rules draw themselves in on load via stroke-dashoffset, establishing structure before content appears.

tell: Centered text, or a decorative accent color used for 'pop' instead of structure.
refuse: Never centers text.
Never uses more than one accent hue.
Never uses a drop shadow.
Never justifies body copy.
mobile_fallback: The grid collapses to a single flush-left column; weight/size hierarchy carries over unchanged; the one accent rule becomes a horizontal divider between sections.
physical_antecedents: Müller-Brockmann concert posters
Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) timetable boards
Zürich tram wayfinding signage

name: Bauhaus
one_line: Primary-color geometric primitives as literal structural units — form states its function.
palette_hint: pure primary red/yellow/blue at high chroma (C0.20-0.30) + true black/white; no tints, no tertiary mixing

type.notes: single geometric sans (Bayer-style geometric or Futura-class) set unjustified in tracked caps for display; no italics; no serif ever.

grammar: Only primary colors (pure red, yellow, blue) plus true black and white appear anywhere in the system.
Circles, squares, and triangles are used as literal structural units (a circle is a container or divider, not decoration).
Type is a single geometric sans, set unjustified, with no italics and no serif ever introduced.
Every shape's size and position is derived from a stated function (a divider, a container, a counterweight) — never placed purely for balance.
first_viewport: A large red circle and a black square overlap in the upper-left quadrant of the viewport against pure white; the headline runs in tracked-out geometric-sans caps along the lower edge, broken by the yellow triangle that punctures its baseline.

motion.moment: The geometric primitives (circle/square/triangle) slide into their final grid position from off-frame on load, arriving in sequence.

tell: Rounded/organic shapes, pastel palette, serif type — any softness at all.
refuse: Never uses a serif.
Never uses more than the primary triad plus black/white.
Never applies a shape as mere decoration — every circle/square/triangle is structural.
mobile_fallback: The geometric primitives stack vertically in their original proportions rather than shrinking; the primary-color blocking becomes full-width horizontal bands.
physical_antecedents: Herbert Bayer's Bauhaus exhibition posters
Marcel Breuer's Wassily chair
the Dessau Bauhaus building's curtain-wall facade

name: De Stijl
one_line: The orthogonal grid itself is the artwork, in flat red/yellow/blue on black-and-white.
palette_hint: flat primary red (H20-30) + yellow (H90-100) + blue (H255-265) blocks on white/black/grey fields, C0.18-0.25, no gradients

type.notes: one geometric/grotesque sans set only in black or a primary-color fill, never grey; caps-only for structural labels; no italics.

grammar: Every line in the composition is strictly horizontal or vertical; no diagonal or curve appears anywhere, including in motion.
Color fills are flat and unmodulated — no gradient, no texture, no shadow.
The grid lines themselves are rendered as visible black rules, not implicit container edges — the grid IS the artwork.
Fields are asymmetric but balanced: a small saturated field can visually counterweight a much larger neutral field.
first_viewport: The viewport is quartered by two black orthogonal rules (one vertical at 38%, one horizontal at 62%) into four unequal fields; one field is flat red, the rest white, and the headline sits inside the smallest field set flush to its own edges.

motion.moment: The orthogonal dividing rules extend from a single point to their full length on load, defining the fields before content fills them.

tell: Any diagonal line, gradient, or off-primary hue.
refuse: Never uses a diagonal or curve.
Never lets a field span less than a full grid cell.
Never introduces a fourth hue beyond red/yellow/blue/black/white/grey.
mobile_fallback: The orthogonal fields stack as full-width horizontal bands in their original color, preserving the asymmetric proportions rather than resizing to equal heights.
physical_antecedents: Rietveld's Red and Blue Chair
the Schröder House facade
Mondrian's studio wall arrangement as photographed by his contemporaries

name: Constructivist / Soviet avant-garde
one_line: Diagonal photomontage and red-on-cream type running as a graphic shape, not just text.
palette_hint: committed red (H20-30, C0.20+) + true black on cream/off-white ground; yellow as the only secondary addition

type.notes: bold condensed display sans that can rotate to follow diagonal composition lines; body reverts to a plain neo-grotesque; no serif, no light weights.

grammar: At least one major compositional element runs on a diagonal axis (rotated 10-25°) rather than the horizontal/vertical grid.
The palette is capped at red, black, and cream/white, with yellow as the only permitted addition.
Type is a condensed/bold sans set as a graphic shape — it can run at an angle or interlock with imagery, never confined to a rectangular text box.
Photography is treated as raw material for photomontage (cropped, layered, recombined), never shown as an untouched single frame.
first_viewport: A photomontage figure is cropped and rotated 15 degrees off the horizontal, red condensed display type runs diagonally across the frame from lower-left to upper-right, and a solid black wedge anchors the opposite corner.

motion.moment: The photomontage element slams in already rotated, with a brief diagonal overshoot correction.
motion.easing: fast ease-out with 5-10 degree overshoot settle, 200-300ms

tell: Horizontal-only layouts, muted palettes, serif type.
refuse: Never uses a horizontal-only composition.
Never uses a soft pastel.
Never sets type outside a diagonal or angled baseline in a hero moment.
mobile_fallback: The diagonal composition rotates to a single steep diagonal band running the height of the screen rather than flattening to horizontal.
physical_antecedents: Rodchenko's Mayakovsky book covers
Lissitzky's 'Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge' poster
a 1920s Soviet agitprop train car

name: Dutch Structuralism (Total Design / Experimental Jetset)
one_line: The grid made visible; deadpan Helvetica captions describe the system itself.
palette_hint: near-achromatic ink-on-paper; structural color (if any) reads as a signal, C0.05-0.10 max, any hue

type.notes: single neutral grotesque (Helvetica/Univers-class) at every size including captions; deadpan tone; no italics, no display face swap.

grammar: The underlying grid is rendered visible (hairline rules, ruler marks, or column guides left on-screen) rather than hidden by whitespace.
Only one typeface family is used system-wide, almost always a neutral grotesque (Helvetica/Univers-class).
Copy voice is deadpan and self-referential — it can describe the design system itself rather than only the product.
No decorative color exists; color, when present, marks structure (a section boundary) not mood.
first_viewport: The page opens on the grid itself: thin black hairlines partition the viewport into a visible column system, the wordmark is set in plain Helvetica at the same size as the body intro, and a caption below the grid states which grid it is.

motion.moment: Almost no motion; the one moment is the grid's hairlines appearing as a flat instant toggle when a caption calls attention to them.

tell: Warm/organic type choices, hidden/invisible grid, marketing-voice copy.
refuse: Never hides the underlying grid.
Never writes marketing-voice copy.
Never uses more than one typeface.
mobile_fallback: The visible grid becomes a single visible column with its hairline rule preserved above each section; the caption about the grid stays.
physical_antecedents: Total Design's Dutch PTT stamps
Wim Crouwel's Stedelijk Museum posters
Experimental Jetset's Whitney Museum identity

name: Memphis
origin: Milan, 1980-1987 — Ettore Sottsass and the Memphis Group
one_line: Clashing neon-and-pastel geometry, deliberately off-grid, refusing a single safe accent.
palette_hint: pastel-and-neon clash: two hues from opposite ends of the wheel at once, e.g. hot pink H340 + acid green H120, both C0.20+

type.notes: mixed weights within a single headline permitted (part of the deliberate clash); geometric or display-grotesque display face; body stays a plain geometric sans for legibility.

grammar: At least two colors from opposite temperature families (a neon and a pastel) appear adjacent in the same composition, deliberately clashing.
Shapes are geometric but placed off the underlying grid at an angle or offset, never grid-aligned.
At least one squiggle, zigzag, or terrazzo-speckle fill pattern appears as a literal graphic element, not a texture overlay.
No single accent color dominates by area — visual weight is distributed across 3+ competing hues.
first_viewport: A hot-pink squiggle and a terrazzo-speckle fill float behind an asymmetrically placed headline set in mismatched weights, with a yellow triangle and a teal circle scattered off-grid in the lower third.

motion.moment: One squiggle or terrazzo shape wobbles/rotates slightly on hover, independent of everything else on the page.

tell: Restrained palette, aligned grid, single accent color.
refuse: Never aligns every shape to the same grid.
Never uses a single restrained accent color.
Never lets the palette read as 'safe.'
mobile_fallback: Shapes reflow into a single column but retain their off-grid rotation and scale; nothing snaps to alignment.
physical_antecedents: Sottsass's Carlton bookcase
a Memphis-era Swatch watch face
an 1980s Milan showroom terrazzo floor

name: Y2K / Frutiger Aero
origin: Global consumer tech, 2004-2013 — Windows XP/Mac OS X-era skeuomorphism
one_line: Glossy aqua gradients and bokeh nature-tech collage — 2004-era optimism, never flat.
palette_hint: aqua/sky-blue/teal gradient family, H180-220, L0.65-0.90, glossy highlight adds a near-white specular band

type.notes: rounded humanist/geometric sans with soft terminals (Frutiger/early-Trebuchet lineage); no condensed or slab anywhere; occasional variable-axis widening for headline drama.

grammar: Every primary surface carries a gloss pass (a highlight gradient or specular sheen), never a flat matte fill.
The palette is anchored in aqua/sky-blue/teal/white; a fully achromatic or fully warm palette never appears.
Corners are rounded on every primary container (pill shapes, bubble buttons) — sharp unrounded corners are reserved for incidental dividers only.
At least one nature-tech collage element (water droplet, bokeh, cloud, or leaf motif rendered with a tech sheen) appears per major surface.
first_viewport: A glossy aqua-to-white gradient sky fills the upper two-thirds of the viewport with a soft bokeh water-droplet overlay, a rounded pill-shaped nav bar floats near the top with a chrome bevel, and the headline sits in a bubble-round humanist sans.

motion.moment: A glossy highlight sweeps across a rounded surface on hover, like light passing over a wet/chrome bevel.

tell: Flat colors, no gloss/highlight layer, matte surfaces.
refuse: Never uses flat, matte fills without a gloss/highlight pass.
Never uses a cold achromatic palette.
Never uses sharp unrounded corners on primary surfaces.
mobile_fallback: The gradient sky and bokeh layer scale to cover the viewport height rather than cropping; the pill nav collapses to a single glossy bar.
physical_antecedents: Windows XP's 'Bliss' desktop wallpaper
an early-2000s iMac G3 shell
a 2005-era MSN Messenger emoticon set

name: Brutalist web
one_line: Raw, unstyled browser defaults left exactly as the browser draws them.
palette_hint: system default: white/near-white bg, black text, unmodified link blue (~H260)

type.notes: the browser's default system font stack, unmodified; default sizes; no custom webfont load; underlines on links preserved.

grammar: Default browser styling (system font stack, default link blue/underline, default focus ring) is left unstyled wherever it appears.
No element carries a border-radius or a box-shadow anywhere in the system.
Layout blocks are unaligned to a symmetric grid on purpose — column widths and gutters vary without a repeating pattern.
No image is used purely for decoration; every image is content.
first_viewport: Default system-serif body text starts at the very top of the page with no hero, an unstyled blue underlined link sits inline in the first sentence, and the browser's default focus ring is visible around the first interactive element.

motion.moment: An abrupt, unapologetic hard-cut state change with no crossfade.

tell: Rounded corners, shadows, smooth transitions anywhere.
refuse: Never adds a border-radius.
Never adds a box-shadow.
Never restyles the default link color/underline.
mobile_fallback: No fallback needed — the layout is already a single unstyled column at any width.
physical_antecedents: a raw poured-concrete municipal building facade
an early-1990s university department homepage
a plain text README file

name: Neo-brutalism (product UI)
origin: Web/product UI, ~2020-present — popularized by Michał Malewicz's March 2022 essay (no single originator is universally credited)
one_line: Thick black borders and flat offset shadows — a rubber stamp pressed into pixels.
palette_hint: flat saturated primary-ish fills (C0.18-0.28) + true black borders/shadows, no gradients

type.notes: headline at 700-900 weight, 2-3x body size, tight-normal tracking; no italics; body in a plain geometric or neo-grotesque sans.

grammar: Every primary container has a solid 2-4px black (or near-black) border with zero blur.
Elevation is expressed as a flat-color offset shadow (translate + solid fill, no blur radius) rather than a soft drop-shadow.
Border-radius is 0 on structural containers — corners are square throughout, with no documented exception.
Headline type runs at a heavy weight (700+), sized dramatically larger than body, with no lighter weight ever used for a headline.
first_viewport: A flat yellow card with a 3px solid black border and a 4px black offset shadow sits top-left holding the headline in 900-weight black type; a second flat-blue card overlaps its bottom edge by 20px with no radius on either.

motion.moment: A button's hard offset shadow presses in to zero-offset on click.
motion.easing: snappy near-linear, mimics a physical stamp, 80-120ms

tell: Blurred shadows, gradients, thin/no borders.
refuse: Never blurs a shadow.
Never uses a border thinner than 2px on a primary container.
Never uses a soft pastel fill.
mobile_fallback: Cards stack full-width; borders and offset shadows stay at full pixel value, never scaled down.
physical_antecedents: a rubber stamp and ink pad
a hazard-yellow warning sign with a thick black border
a comic-book panel gutter

name: Japanese editorial (Idea magazine / MUJI)
origin: Tokyo, 1980-present — MUJI's product and print design language. (Idea magazine, the namesake 1953 typography journal, in fact runs a more colorful, maximalist editorial register per its own citation below; this card follows the MUJI/negative-space lineage specifically, not Idea's editorial pages.)
one_line: Negative space as an active element; hand-tuned kerning carries the hierarchy.
palette_hint: near-monochrome (C0-0.02) plus one muted natural material tone (wood/paper, H30-50, C0.03-0.06)

type.notes: one humanist sans hand-kerned per block; generous line-height (1.8-2.2); weight (not size) carries hierarchy; no bold overuse.

grammar: Negative space occupies a majority of at least one major section per screen and is never filled to 'balance' the layout.
Kerning and line-height are tuned per block rather than left at a default, aiming at a visibly deliberate vertical rhythm.
The MUJI/negative-space register keeps color near-monochrome plus one natural material tone — this is a distinct, more restrained register than Idea magazine's own colorful editorial spreads.
Type weight, more than size, commonly carries hierarchy — headline and body can share a similar size with weight differing.
first_viewport: Roughly 70% of the viewport is empty near-white space; a single vertical hairline sits at the right third, and a small, precisely kerned caption-sized headline anchors the lower-left corner beside one muted wood-tone rule.

motion.moment: A single element's opacity resolves slowly as it enters the negative space; nothing else on the page moves at the same time.

tell: Dense copy with no breathing room, saturated color.
refuse: Never fills negative space 'just because it's empty.'
Never uses more than one saturated accent.
Never sets body copy at a tight line-height.
mobile_fallback: The negative-space ratio is preserved by increasing top/bottom margin rather than shrinking it; the single accent rule stays inset from the edge.
physical_antecedents: a MUJI product label
an Idea magazine spread
a traditional shoji screen's negative-space proportion

name: Scandinavian functionalism
origin: Nordic countries, 1930s-present — Stockholm Exhibition 1930; Aalto, Jacobsen
one_line: Light birch and pale grey, generous margins, ornament only where it states a function.
palette_hint: pale birch/oat neutrals (H40-60, C0.02-0.05) with at most one moderate accent, C0.10-0.15

type.notes: warm humanist sans, regular/medium weights only; bold reserved for true emphasis; generous leading throughout.

grammar: The base palette stays in light wood/white/pale-grey tones; a saturated hue, when used, covers no more than one small accent role.
Margins and gutters are generous by a fixed multiple (at least 1.5x a typical dense-layout equivalent) at every breakpoint.
Type is a humanist (not geometric-cold) sans, set at moderate weight — bold is reserved for true emphasis, never default.
Every ornamental element states a function (a rule marks a section, a shape marks a category) — nothing is placed purely for decoration.
first_viewport: A pale birch-toned background holds a single softly-lit product photograph centered-left, with generous margin on all sides and a quiet humanist-sans headline set small and left-aligned beneath it.

motion.moment: A product photo's ambient light appears to shift very subtly on load (a soft cross-fade between two exposures).

tell: Dark themes, saturated color, ornamental flourish.
refuse: Never defaults to dark mode as primary.
Never uses more than two accent hues.
Never adds ornament that doesn't state a function.
mobile_fallback: The product photo and caption stack full-width with the same generous margin ratio, never reduced to save space.
physical_antecedents: an Alvar Aalto vase
a pale birch Arne Jacobsen chair
a Nordic apartment window with sheer curtains and low winter light

name: Italian Rationalist / Radical design
one_line: An infinite black-on-white grid receding to a vanishing point, punctured by one red intrusion.
palette_hint: true black/white grid with one saturated intrusion, usually red H20-30 C0.20+

type.notes: monumental tracked caps in neo-grotesque or condensed sans for the rationalist register; plain typewriter mono for the radical-manifesto register — pick one, never mix.

grammar: A strict orthogonal or radially-symmetric grid underlies the whole composition, visible even where content interrupts it.
The palette stays predominantly black-and-white, with one or a small number of saturated intrusions (Radical-era work sometimes uses several kitsch colors at once).
Photography, when used, is deadpan and documentary in tone, never lifestyle-warm or candid.
Scale is monumental — at least one element is rendered far larger than its informational weight would require, as a rhetorical gesture.
first_viewport: An infinite black-on-white grid recedes toward a vanishing point behind the headline, which sits centered and monumental in tracked caps, with a single red rule intruding across the grid at one horizontal band.

motion.moment: The infinite grid appears to recede further on scroll, as if the vanishing point moves with the viewer.

tell: Warm/organic photography, asymmetric informality.
refuse: Never breaks the grid with an organic curve.
Never uses warm lifestyle photography.
Never uses more than one saturated intrusion color.
mobile_fallback: The infinite grid renders as a repeating vertical band pattern behind a single scrolling column of content.
physical_antecedents: Terragni's Casa del Fascio facade
Superstudio's 'Continuous Monument' photomontage
a 1970s Italian design-theory journal spread

name: Mid-century American corporate
one_line: One geometric motif repeated at every scale, anchored by a confident flat logotype.
palette_hint: 2-3 confident flat hues (often navy H250-260, red H20-30, cream ground), C0.15-0.22, no gradients

type.notes: single confident geometric-sans logotype-derived display face; humanist sans for body; no italics; tight consistent baseline.

grammar: The system uses exactly one recurring geometric motif (a circle, a stripe, a diagonal band) repeated at every scale from logotype to section divider.
Illustration, where used, stays flat and graphic — no photorealistic rendering, no gradient shading.
The logotype/wordmark sits as the fixed visual anchor of the first viewport, never competing with a larger hero image.
Color blocking is confident and flat — no gradient, no texture, exactly 2-3 named colors per composition.
first_viewport: A bold circular red logotype anchors the upper-left corner against a cream field; a confident diagonal band in navy sweeps from that corner to the lower-right, carrying the headline in a single geometric-sans weight.

motion.moment: The circular logotype spins a quarter-turn into its resting position on load, echoing a Saul Bass title-sequence cut.

tell: Photographic realism, gradient/glass effects.
refuse: Never uses a gradient.
Never uses more than one geometric motif system-wide.
Never lets illustration become photorealistic.
mobile_fallback: The diagonal band becomes a single angled divider at the top of the stacked column; the logotype stays fixed-size, never shrinks below legibility.
physical_antecedents: the IBM logo on a 1960s mainframe cabinet
Saul Bass's Bell System logo on a payphone
an ABC television station ident card
avoid_for: cutting-edge tech startups wanting to feel new

name: Op-art
origin: 1960s — Bridget Riley, Victor Vasarely; MoMA's 'The Responsive Eye' 1965
one_line: A single mathematical pattern engineered to vibrate — the pattern is the entire content.
palette_hint: strict black/white or a very narrow value range, C near 0

type.notes: minimal incidental captions in one weight only, geometric sans, small size — type never competes with the pattern's optical field.

grammar: A single repeating geometric pattern (lines, dots, or checks) covers the entire compositional field, engineered so adjacent elements' value contrast creates optical vibration.

The palette stays within a narrow value range — most often strict black/white, though some op-art (e.g. Vasarely) works in a narrow chromatic range instead — no mid-tone relief is introduced to 'calm' the pattern.
No photographic or illustrative content is layered on top of the pattern field; the pattern IS the content.
Line/shape repetition follows a mathematical progression (constant spacing or a defined ratio), never hand-varied.
first_viewport: The entire viewport is filled edge-to-edge with a tight black-and-white concentric-line pattern that appears to pulse at the center; the only content is a small caption-weight label set in the pattern's one calm gap.

motion.moment: The pattern itself subtly animates via a moiré shift tied to mouse position or scroll, as the entire interaction.
motion.easing: continuous, tied to input position, not click-triggered

tell: Soft gradients, organic asymmetry, muted contrast.
refuse: Never layers 'content' on top of the pattern.
Never softens the value contrast.
Never uses an organic/hand-drawn line.
mobile_fallback: The pattern's line frequency is reduced (fewer, thicker lines) to avoid moiré aliasing on small screens, preserving the pulse effect rather than the exact density.
physical_antecedents: Bridget Riley's 'Movement in Squares' canvas
a moiré-pattern venetian blind
a barbershop pole

name: Psychedelic (Fillmore poster)
origin: San Francisco, 1965-1971 — Wes Wilson, Victor Moscoso, the Fillmore Auditorium
one_line: Melting hand-lettered type fused into Art-Nouveau illustration at full complementary saturation.
palette_hint: full-saturation complementary pairs (e.g. orange H40 vs blue H240), C0.22-0.32, no neutral relief

type.notes: display type is illustrated/hand-lettered (not a real font swap), integrated into the artwork; body copy reverts to a plain humanist sans for actual reading.

grammar: Display type is deliberately distorted (melting, warping, or interlocking) to the point of reduced legibility, and integrates into the illustration rather than sitting in a separate text box.
At least two complementary hues (e.g., orange/blue, red/green) appear at full saturation adjacent to each other with no neutral relief between them.
Illustrated line work is organic and flowing (Art-Nouveau-derived), never geometric or ruler-straight.
No grid discipline governs placement — composition is filled edge-to-edge by the illustration's own logic.
first_viewport: Hand-lettered, melting display type in vibrating orange-on-magenta fills the upper half of the viewport, its letterforms integrated into an Art-Nouveau-derived illustrated border that frames the entire composition.

motion.moment: The hand-lettered display type appears to 'melt' — a slow vertical distortion settling into its final shape on load.

tell: Legible geometric sans, neutral palette, grid discipline.
refuse: Never lets the display type stay perfectly legible.
Never uses a neutral/restrained palette.
Never separates type from illustration.
mobile_fallback: The illustrated border collapses to a top-and-bottom band only (dropping the side borders) so the hand-lettered headline keeps full width.
physical_antecedents: a 1966 Fillmore Auditorium concert handbill
a Grateful Dead LP gatefold
a black-light poster shop window

name: Punk / zine (Jamie Reid)
one_line: Ransom-note cut-and-paste lettering on photocopier-degraded black and white.
palette_hint: pure black/white photocopy contrast, one shock spot color (often red or hazard yellow) at C0.20+

type.notes: headline mixes 3+ sizes/weights/faces within one line (literal ransom-note assembly); body in plain typewriter-style or default serif, photocopier-degraded look.

grammar: At least one headline mixes 3+ different type sizes/weights/faces within a single word or line, assembled like cut newspaper lettering.
Contrast is pushed to pure black/white (no midtone greys) to simulate photocopier degradation.
At least one element references physical damage or assembly (a torn edge, a visible tape strip, a staple mark) rendered as a real graphic, not a filter.
Alignment is deliberately imperfect — baselines and margins vary line to line rather than snapping to a shared grid.
first_viewport: Ransom-note headline type — each letter a different cut-out size and face — is taped across a photocopier-degraded black-and-white photograph, with a strip of visible packing-tape texture along one torn edge.

motion.moment: Elements slam into place abruptly with a slight rotation-settle, echoing pasted-down cut paper.

tell: Consistent type system, clean vector reproduction.
refuse: Never uses a single consistent typeface across a headline.
Never smooths the photocopy contrast to greyscale.
Never aligns elements to a clean grid.
mobile_fallback: The ransom-note headline reflows letter-by-letter with the same mixed sizes, allowed to wrap raggedly rather than resizing to fit one line.
physical_antecedents: a Sex Pistols 'God Save the Queen' single sleeve
a photocopied fanzine stapled at a kitchen table
a safety-pin-and-tape flyer stapled to a lamppost

name: Terminal / hacker
one_line: Monospace-only, phosphor-on-black, a blinking cursor as the literal interface metaphor.
palette_hint: single phosphor hue (green H130-140 or amber H50-60) at high L/moderate C on true black

type.notes: single monospace face throughout, including body copy; tabular figures mandatory; no proportional fallback; block-cursor character as a literal element.

grammar: Every piece of type on the page is monospace; no proportional font ever appears, including in body copy.
The palette is capped at one phosphor color (green or amber) plus black; no other hue is introduced.
A blinking block cursor or equivalent (▌) appears at least once as a literal UI element, not a decorative afterthought.
Interaction is framed as command input (a $ or > prompt) even where the underlying control is a button or link.
first_viewport: A black viewport opens on a single monospace prompt line with a blinking block cursor; a boot-sequence-style list of status lines prints above it in phosphor green, then the primary command input appears at the bottom.

motion.moment: Text renders as if typed character-by-character on key state changes only, not everywhere.
motion.easing: monospace-stepped, cursor blink at a fixed interval

tell: Proportional/sans-serif type, soft shadows, rounded UI chrome.
refuse: Never uses a proportional font.
Never uses a rounded corner.
Never lets a color exist outside the phosphor/amber/black set.
mobile_fallback: Panes stack vertically in command order rather than side-by-side; the outer shell still doesn't scroll — each pane scrolls independently within its own fixed height.
physical_antecedents: an IBM 3270 green-phosphor terminal
a VT100 console
a 1980s BBS login screen

name: Industrial / datasheet
one_line: Hairline-ruled tables, decimal-aligned tabular figures, labeled technical diagrams instead of photos.
palette_hint: monochrome ink-on-paper plus 1-2 spot colors (safety orange H40-50 or signal blue H230-240) for status only

type.notes: monospace/tabular-figure numerals decimal-aligned; neo-grotesque sans for field labels; no italics anywhere; consistent units column.

grammar: Every table and data grouping uses hairline rules (1px solid) for structure; no box-shadow or card container ever separates a data block.
All numerals are set in a monospace or tabular-figure face and decimal-aligned within their column.
At least one labeled technical diagram (exploded view, dimension callout, or schematic) replaces what would otherwise be lifestyle photography.
The palette is monochrome or capped at two spot colors, used only for signal/status, never for branding decoration.
first_viewport: A hairline-ruled table fills the viewport with no hero image; the leftmost column holds a labeled technical diagram, and every numeral column to its right is monospace and decimal-aligned.

motion.moment: A table row's value updates with a brief monospace digit-roll, echoing a mechanical counter.

tell: Lifestyle photography, marketing superlatives, loose alignment.
refuse: Never uses a card with a shadow.
Never uses more than two spot colors.
Never leaves a numeral column unaligned.

palette_hint: flat single-hue-family fills (e.g. all-lavender or all-peach figures) with exactly one flat shadow tone; skin tones abstracted to non-representational hues

type.notes: a rounded geometric sans is used everywhere; the illustration, not the type, carries the brand voice.

grammar: Human figures render limbless or with noodle-thin, boneless limbs and oversized heads/hands.
Fills are flat, single-hue-family, with exactly one flat (non-gradient) shadow shape per figure.
Scenes depict generic 'collaboration' or 'productivity' scenarios with no specific, observed detail.
Figures float in undefined negative space with no ground plane or environment logic.
Diversity is signaled only through skin-tone palette swaps on an identical body template, never through pose, body type, or context variation.
materials: digital vector illustration only — no analog/print antecedent
first_viewport: A hero section pairs a bold rounded-sans headline with a large flat-illustration scene of interchangeable limbless figures collaborating around an oversized laptop or clipboard, floating in empty colored negative space.

motion.moment: figures gently bob or a single element (a coffee cup, a plant) idly loops — the same idle-loop trick used across nearly every SaaS site that adopts this world
forbidden: nothing is meaningfully forbidden within the world itself — its motion, like its illustration, is the convergent default being catalogued for refusal

tell: this world *is* the tell — any use of it signals template SaaS rather than a considered choice; recognize a request like 'add a hero illustration of people collaborating' and route to a physical-object-derived alternative instead.
refuse: generating this world for any project — recommend a physical-object-derived alternative instead
softening the figures further (rounder corners, softer pastels) as a 'fix' — the whole lineage is the anti-pattern, not one attribute of it
mobile_fallback: not applicable — not recommended as a target world at any viewport
physical_antecedents: none — this is a purely digital-native illustration convention with no physical print or material antecedent, part of why it reads as placeholder rather than crafted
avoid_for: every context — catalog only to help the model recognize and reject it on sight

type.notes: mixed weights and even mixed families within a single word are expected; type overlaps imagery and other type at illegible densities on purpose; legible body copy reverts to a plain typewriter/system face as ironic contrast to the chaos above it.

grammar: Type deliberately overlaps other type or imagery to the point of partial illegibility — this is a choice, not a bug.
At least one torn-paper, distressed, or degraded-photocopy texture layer sits over every major image.
Mixed type weights or families appear within a single word or headline, never a consistent type scale.
Every composition bleeds off at least one edge asymmetrically — no centered, contained layouts.
Photography is treated as raw texture (cropped, degraded, layered) rather than a clean editorial image.
first_viewport: A headline built from mismatched, overlapping type weights bleeds off two edges of the viewport, laid over a degraded, torn-edge photographic texture, with no visible grid or alignment system.

motion.moment: elements slam into place with a slight rotational overshoot then settle, as if physically pasted down and jostled

clean, undegraded photography

name: Vintage Analog / Retro Film

type.notes: captions and small metadata set in a typewriter-feeling monospace or a warm slab serif; nothing sans-serif-only appears for captions, echoing physical print-back stamping.

Regulatory/fine-print text renders at a defined minimum legible size and sits in a visible, non-collapsed location, never hidden behind a 'learn more' toggle.
Interactive targets meet a large minimum hit-area size across the entire system, prioritizing accessibility over density.
Contrast ratios exceed the standard minimum (targeting AAA-level, not just AA) on all text, including fine print.

name: Field Guide Naturalist

A color-coded edge tab or strip system marks category/family, consistent across every page.
Common name sets in a plain serif; scientific/Latin binomial sets in italic directly beneath or beside it, and this pairing never breaks.
Illustration, not photography, carries the primary identification content; photography, if present, is supplementary only.
